title: Decision Framing Laboratory
summary: Make four decisions about stock at risk, two of them described as gains and two as losses. Nothing is revealed until all four are made.
learningObjectives: State what a framing effect is in terms of a reference point.
Explain why the certainty of the safe option matters independently of its safety.
Distinguish a robust aggregate shift from a claim about any individual.
Rewrite a decision problem so that the framing asymmetry is smaller.
Say why a framing effect is not by itself evidence of irrationality.
interactionTypes: side-by-side reframing of each decision made
bar chart paired with a data table
constructive rewriting challenge with live output
privacy: No data collected, stored or transmitted; decisions stay in the browser tab as JavaScript variables and disappear on reload, and nothing is written to storage.
accessibilityNotes: Nothing in this tool is timed and nothing moves; there is no CSS animation or transition anywhere, so a reduced-motion preference has nothing to switch off. The two options are large text blocks rather than small controls, because each carries a sentence that has to be read before choosing; each is labelled Option A or Option B in words as well as carrying its own description. Nothing depends on colour: the chart bars print their own percentages and the loss-framed bars are hatched as well as differently filled, and the reveal sets the two framings side by side as text. The chart is aria-hidden and paired inside the same figure with a four-column table. The challenge uses native checkboxes with visible labels and per-item text feedback, and the rewritten scenario it produces is rendered as ordinary readable text. Every control has an accessible name, headings do not skip, focus moves to the results heading and to the first option of each scenario, and forced-colours rules are supplied for the scenario card, the reframe panels and the chart. Usable at 320px and at projector widths with no horizontal page scroll; wide tables scroll inside their own containers.
readmeTopic: Framing and reference dependence: identical arithmetic, two descriptions, different choices
simulationNotes: The four scenarios are fictional and deliberately contain no people, so that nothing turns on how a reader feels about the stakes - which is also why the limits panel says nothing here generalises to decisions where the stakes are the point. Every stock is divisible by 27 (810, 540, 1080 and 1620) so that all quantities are whole numbers: the safe option saves exactly a third of the stock, the very-likely version offers a 90 per cent chance of saving a third divided by 0.9, and the gamble offers a 1 in 3 chance of saving everything. All three have the same expected outcome. Frames are assigned at random, two gains and two losses, so each scenario is seen once and no within-person comparison is possible; the reveal therefore prints the unseen framing beside each decision. The reference-point setting changes no number and is deliberately not modelled in the worked example, because inventing a small effect would be worse than reporting none; the results prose says so and turns it into a question about which reference point the learner actually used. The worked example is simulated with mulberry32 seed 20261011: 300 fictional participants in each certainty condition making four decisions each, so 600 decisions per cell, with the safe option chosen at rates of 0.74 and 0.52 in the gain frame and 0.33 and 0.27 in the loss frame for the certain and very-likely versions. It produces 74, 53, 33 and 29 per cent. Both the framing effect and the certainty effect are built in to illustrate two well-replicated findings; they are not evidence for them, not norms and not anybody's data, and the debrief is explicit that replication size varies with wording, sample and domain.
